title: AI and Jobs in 2030: 3 Anthropic Institute Scenarios (2026)
summary: Will AI take jobs by 2030? Three scenarios from an Anthropic Institute paper, every number sourced: GDP, wages, labor share and unemployment. Not forecasts.
body_markdown:
Will AI take jobs by 2030? A September 2026 economic model of that question gives three answers, not one. In September 2026, an Anthropic Institute working paper put unemployment among US cognitive workers at the start of 2030 at **2.9%, 4.5% or 17.9%** , in a modest, a substantial and an extreme scenario. The authors attach no probability to any of them.


The paper, "Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI" by Anton Korinek, Charles I. Jones, Szymon Sacher, Tess Cotter and Peter McCrory, is a framework, not a forecast. It turns a few assumptions about AI into paths for GDP, wages, the labor share and unemployment, so that people who disagree can see exactly which assumption they disagree about.


This post explains the main tables of the paper (Tables 1 to 6) with their printed pages, sets the paper beside other published AI jobs estimates and the history of automation, and reads it next to Dario Amodei's essay "Machines of Loving Grace" from October 2024, with its "powerful AI", its "country of geniuses in a datacenter" and its "compressed 21st century". It ends with what a worker, a founder and a small team can do with the answer.


> **TL;DR:** An Anthropic Institute paper models three US economies at the start of 2030. GDP is 1.6%, 8.3% or 32.4% above a world with no AI, and cognitive unemployment is 2.9%, 4.5% or 17.9%. The authors say these are not predictions. The 2024 Amodei essay is a conditional prediction with a separate clock.[Read the paper](https://assets.claude.com/cf58f84d46a4a76bf5a5b039ac695fba6b80041c.pdf)


### 🔑 Key Takeaways


- **Three scenarios, no forecast.** "The scenarios are not predictions, and we attach no probabilities to them" (p. 3). The views are the five authors' and "do not necessarily represent the views of Anthropic" (p. 1).
- **The range is wide.** By the start of 2030, cognitive employment is 0.5%, 3.9% or 21.5% below its mid-2026 level, and the cognitive unemployment rate is 2.9%, 4.5% or 17.9% (Table 3, p. 31).
- **Pay moves apart.** In the extreme scenario, cognitive wages are 11.5% below the no-AI path and wages in all other occupations 33.6% above it (p. 31).
- **The gain goes to capital.** The labor share falls from 60% to 45.2% in the extreme case, labor income ends 0.5% above the no-AI path, and capital income 81.4% above it (p. 31). A transfer of about 9% of GDP would keep cognitive income whole (p. 35).
- **The public lands in the middle.** Run on the answers of the 3,259 survey respondents who answered all five items, the model gives a median GDP 8.6% above the no-AI path and cognitive employment 4.2% lower (Table 4, p. 36).
- **The data cannot tell yet.** The scenarios separate mostly after 2027 (pp. 4 and 38), and labor studies with data through August 2026 find no clear AI effect on unemployment ([Yale Budget Lab](https://budgetlab.yale.edu/sites/default/files/page_to_pdf/1419/publication_1419.pdf) ).
- **The essay is a different object.** "Machines of Loving Grace" is a best case "if everything goes right", and its 5 to 10 years start only when powerful AI exists.

## 📊 AI and Jobs in 2030 at a Glance


**A September 2026 working paper models three US economies at the start of 2030. GDP is 1.6%, 8.3% or 32.4% above an economy with no AI, and unemployment among cognitive workers is 2.9%, 4.5% or 17.9% (Table 3, p. 31). The scenarios differ in the pace of AI and in its disruptiveness (p. 22).**


Read four caveats before the numbers:


- **Not forecasts.** "The scenarios are not predictions, and we attach no probabilities to them" (p. 3).
- **The authors' views.** The title page says the views "are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the views of Anthropic or The Anthropic Institute" (p. 1).
- **One country.** The model is calibrated on US labor data, and the survey asked US adults (pp. 25, 26 and 29).
- **"Cognitive" is the paper's own category.** It means "management, professional, sales, and office jobs" (p. 3), twelve occupation groups that employ 62.4% of workers in the 2025 Current Population Survey (p. 25). Every other occupation, from electricians to nurses' aides, sits in a second group that AI does not touch directly in the model.


The diagram shows how the two kinds of input lead to the three scenarios, each with its cognitive unemployment rate at the start of 2030.


The two input boxes follow the paper's own split (p. 22). The pace of AI covers how many tasks AI can affect, how widely it is used and the gain per task. Disruptiveness covers the automation share, new human tasks and the ease of switching jobs. The paper calls the modest case "a small technology" (p. 31), the substantial case "more significant than the internet" (p. 32), and says the extreme case goes "well beyond any event in history" (p. 34).

## 🏛️ What Is the "Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI" Paper?


**"Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI" is The Anthropic Institute Working Paper No. 2026-02, dated September 2026, by Anton Korinek, Charles I. Jones, Szymon Sacher, Tess Cotter and Peter McCrory (p. 1). It builds one model of the US economy and runs it under three sets of assumptions about AI, from 2026 to the start of 2030.**


**The problem the paper solves.** The authors start from a plain complaint about the debate. Published estimates of the effect of AI on productivity "span orders of magnitude", and forecasts of its effect on employment "range from negligible to catastrophic" (p. 3). Many of those estimates "are based on differing analytical frameworks, which makes the projections hard to compare" (p. 3).


The paper's answer is one framework with a small set of inputs: "chiefly, what fraction of tasks in the economy are affected by AI, how widely AI is used, how large the productivity gains per task are, and how much AI automates versus augments labor" (p. 3). Two people who disagree about AI can enter their own values and see exactly which input drives the gap. The authors call this "a structured way to compare possibilities for our economic future" (p. 3).


**Scope: what the model covers**


- **Horizon.** From a mid-2026 anchor to the start of 2030 (Table 1, p. 23). The model covers "only the effects of AI on cognitive tasks" and leaves out "rapid advances in robotics", and "Largely for this reason, we do not extend the analysis beyond 2030" (p. 5).
- **Two groups of occupations.** Cognitive occupations "whose work may be directly affected by AI", and "all other occupations, which are not directly exposed (construction workers or electricians, for example)" (p. 3).
- **A base year.** The model starts in 2024, "the last year before the use of large language models spread" (p. 9). For how those models work, see[How Do LLMs Work?](https://www.taskade.com/blog/how-do-llms-work) .


The paper places each scenario against published estimates. The comparison section below shows that list beside other published AI jobs numbers.


### The public scenario explorer


Anthropic publishes the model as an interactive page,["Scenarios for our Economic Future"](https://www.anthropic.com/institute/econ-scenarios) . The paper says the explorer "lets anyone set the parameters and see the paths they imply" (p. 38). On November 25, 2026, the page showed five inputs, and it labels the two groups "Knowledge workers" and "All other workers". The paper confirms that "knowledge work" is the explorer's name for the work of the cognitive occupations (p. 29).

## ⚙️ How Does the Model Work, in Plain Words?


**The model breaks the economy into tasks and each task into single pieces of work. AI lowers the cost of some pieces. A firm gives each piece to the cheaper of a worker or capital. Automated pieces move their whole wage bill to capital, and displaced workers must search for jobs elsewhere, which takes time.**


**Tasks and task instances.** The paper's unit is the task instance. "A task is a type of work, such as reviewing a contract or taking a patient's history. An instance is a single performance of a task, for example one contract review" (p. 8). AI does not take over a whole task at once: "AI arrives instance by instance: some contracts are reviewed with AI while others are not" (p. 8).


Two numbers describe how far AI has spread. The affected mass m is the share of the economy's tasks that AI affects. The diffusion share d is the share of those tasks' instances that people actually perform with AI. Their product, m × d, is "the fraction of the economy's task instances that AI performs" (pp. 10 and 11).


### Automation and augmentation


An instance performed with AI takes one of two forms (p. 11):


- **Augmentation.** AI raises "a worker's labor productivity" on that instance. The worker keeps the instance and the wage for it.
- **Automation.** "an AI system performs the instance outright, so that the instance is performed by capital".


The automation share (` ψ` ) is the fraction of AI-performed instances that are automated. "The technology determines whether an instance is automated or augmented, and firms take this as given" (p. 11). In either form, the unit cost falls by the same gain a. That is why the gain in measured productivity does not depend on the automation share, while the split of income does (p. 12). The difference is the same one that separates an agent from a copilot: see[Agents vs Copilots](https://www.taskade.com/blog/agents-vs-copilots) .


The diagram follows one instance. The key sentence is the paper's: "The entire wage bill of an automated instance moves to capital, however small the cost saving that motivated the switch" (p. 13). In the model, layoffs happen for the cognitive group as a whole: firms lay off the workers they no longer demand at a wage that adjusts slowly (pp. 18 and 19).


**Capital is slow.** In the long run, "in standard neoclassical models, capital is perfectly elastic, since new machines can always be built", so all gains go to wages. Between 2026 and 2030, "capital is less elastic and slower to adjust, so some of the productivity gains show up as a higher return to the owners of capital" (p. 6). The model sets the elasticity of capital supply at` ε` = 3, half the value of the study it builds on (p. 10). The authors lean high "because the capital that performs automated cognitive work is disproportionately compute, financed in a world market and built in a year or two" (p. 26). For that compute, see[AI Data Centers Explained](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-data-centers-explained) .


**Wages are slow.** "If firms are slow to reduce wages, relative wages decline less and the fall in demand shows up instead as lower employment in the cognitive occupations" (p. 7). The paper cites evidence on both sides: for workers who keep their jobs, "base wages reset about once a year and nominal cuts are rare", while workers who change jobs see wages move with productivity (p. 28). It sets the rigidity` ξ` = 0.5, "a half-life of one year" (p. 28). The section on capital and wage rigidity shows what happens at other values.


### Search: why switching jobs takes time


The paper's example is "a software engineer may find it difficult to become an electrician" (p. 3). A displaced worker searches in both groups, but search in the other group counts at a discount, the search discount (` μ` ) (p. 20). The normal-times facts come from the Current Population Survey (p. 26):


- Each month, 22% of unemployed workers found a job.
- 19% of job-finders from cognitive occupations took a job in the all-other group.
- 11% of job-finders from all other occupations took a cognitive job.
- Overall, 14.3% changed group.


Crossing rates differ inside the cognitive group. "unemployed sales and office workers take a job outside the cognitive occupations 28 percent of the time while managers and professionals do so only 10 percent of the time" (p. 28). A discount fitted to managers and professionals would be about 0.09, which is one reason the substantial scenario uses 0.08 (p. 28).


The diagram shows one forward path. In the model, a searcher can also be hired back into a cognitive job, and "a worker hired into group j counts as a j worker from then on" (p. 20). Unemployment rises by the workers that cognitive occupations release "less the number all other occupations have absorbed" (p. 28).


**The ideas channel, and why it is small.** AI also speeds up research, because a research budget that is a share of GDP grows with GDP (p. 16). The authors call the size of this channel "One surprising finding": the growth speedup "is relatively minor, even in the extreme change scenario", because "research remains bottlenecked by physical tasks" (p. 4). In the extreme scenario, the stock of ideas is 0.61% above the no-AI path by 2030 (Table 3, p. 31). The model omits some feedback between research and automation, so "the innovation effects here are likely a lower bound" (p. 4). For AI that does science, see[Scientist AI Explained](https://www.taskade.com/blog/scientist-ai-explained) .


### A worked example: the substantial scenario in 2030


The paper walks through one calculation in plain arithmetic (pp. 12 and 13):

```text
Share of the economy's tasks AI affects        m = 0.30
Share of their instances used with AI          d = 0.40
Share of task instances AI performs        m x d = 0.12
Cut in unit cost per AI instance (logs)        a = 0.45
Labor share before AI                              0.6


Measured TFP   0.6 x 0.30 x 0.40 x 0.45 = 0.032   about 3 percent
exact solution 0.029
Wage gain if the rental rate stays put     m x d x a = 0.054
Rental rate at epsilon = 3                 4.6% above its no-AI level
Capital's term                             0.4 x 0.045 = 0.018
Wage                                       1.9% above the no-AI path,

```


Read it top to bottom. AI performs 12% of the economy's task instances and cuts their cost by 0.45 log points, about 57% more output per instance (p. 32). That adds about 3% to measured productivity. Because capital is scarce in the short run, its owners take part of the gain, and the wage rises 1.9% instead of 5.5% (p. 13). This is a first-order illustration. Table 3 reports the model's full solution with the labor market: an average wage 2.1% above the no-AI path (p. 31).

Firm shares overstate instance shares, "because adopters use it on few tasks and on only some instances of each", so the anchor is 0.10 (p. 27).

**Reinstatement, 0.50 to 0.** The paper cites Acemoglu and Restrepo (2019): new tasks "roughly kept pace with automated ones" from 1947 to 1987 and "ran at about half of them" from 1987 to 2017 (p. 28). The modest value of 0.5 "is thus similar to recent history". The extreme value of 0 "assumes that AI does not create any new tasks for humans to perform" (p. 28). For how past waves of automation created new work, see[The History of Automation](https://www.taskade.com/blog/automation-history) .


**Search and posting.** "Neither can be estimated precisely, given that AI has not yet displaced a significant share of workers" (p. 28). The posting speed "closes a tenth, a quarter, and a half of the all-other group's shortfall per month" (p. 28).

## 🔮 Will AI Take Jobs by 2030? The Three Scenarios (Table 3)


**In all three scenarios, AI moves work out of cognitive occupations and into all other occupations. The scenarios disagree about size and speed (p. 38). By 2030, cognitive employment is 0.5%, 3.9% or 21.5% below its mid-2026 level, and the cognitive unemployment rate is 2.9%, 4.5% or 17.9% (p. 31).**


Read the units with care. Rows marked "above the no-AI path" compare each scenario with an economy that grows 2% a year with no AI (p. 10). The cognitive employment row is a change since mid-2026. The unemployment rows are rates. **The 21.5% and the 17.9% have different bases.** The 21.5% is the percent change in cognitive employment since mid-2026. The 17.9% is the unemployment rate of workers who began in cognitive occupations, as a percent of that group's labor force (Figure 4 note, p. 34, and p. 35).

### The modest change scenario


**In the modest scenario, "AI is a small technology", and the economy continues on a normal path "with AI making changes around the margins" (p. 31).** The paper writes that "just 4 percent of the tasks in the economy have been impacted by AI", in part because of modest capabilities and in part because of slow diffusion (pp. 31 and 32). For every two tasks that AI automates, one new task appears for cognitive labor (p. 32).


GDP is 1.6% above the no-AI path, "an extra ten months of ordinary growth accumulated over four years", and growth is 2.4% a year instead of 2% (p. 32). The cognitive wage is 0.4% higher. Cognitive unemployment stays at 2.9% (Table 3, p. 31), and all-worker unemployment is 3.9% against a normal 3.8% (p. 32). The abstract sums it up: AI "adds less than half a point to GDP growth by 2030 and raises unemployment by a tenth of a point" (p. 1). The conclusion says AI acts like a "normal technology" here (p. 38).


### The substantial change scenario


**In the substantial scenario, "AI is a pivotal technology, more significant than the internet" (p. 32).** In 2030, "12 percent of the tasks in the economy" (roughly 20 percent of the tasks performed by cognitive workers in 2025) "have been impacted by AI" (p. 32). Three quarters of the affected instances are automated, and for every four tasks that AI automates, one new task appears (p. 32).


GDP is 8.3% above the no-AI path, and growth reaches 5.4% a year. "For comparison, the fastest GDP growth rate during the 1990s dot-com boom was 4.7 percent in 1999" (p. 33). The average wage rises only 2.1%, much less than GDP (p. 33). Cognitive employment is 3.9% below its mid-2026 level, employment in all other occupations rises 4.6%, and the cognitive unemployment rate goes from 2.9% to 4.5%, "more than a 50 percent increase" (p. 34).


### The extreme change scenario


**In the extreme scenario, "AI transforms the economy. The macroeconomic consequences go well beyond any event in history, both in terms of magnitudes and in terms of the speed at which change happens" (p. 34).** By 2030, "30 percent of the tasks in the economy" (roughly half of the tasks performed by cognitive workers in 2025) "have been impacted by AI" (p. 34). The abstract describes this as "AI performing almost half of today's cognitive work by 2030" (p. 1). 90% of affected instances are automated, and the paper sets new human tasks to zero (p. 34).


GDP is 40% higher than in mid-2026 and 32% above the no-AI path. Growth reaches "an unprecedented 15.4 percent per year". "If this rate were sustained, per capita incomes would double every five years, compared with doubling every 35 years in the US over the past century" (p. 34).

**The two-group logic.** In the long run, the model has a single wage, and "it typically rises as a result of AI" (pp. 6 and 7). In the medium run, "AI reduces the demand for cognitive labor by automating its tasks", and that shows up "as lower wages and lower employment in cognitive occupations (relative to the paths they would have taken without AI)" (p. 7).


The all-other group works the other way. AI does not change the productivity of its tasks, so their cost depends on the wage alone. Demand for that labor "rises one for one with output and falls with the wage" (p. 14). **The weak link.** Tasks in the model are complements, with an elasticity of substitution (` σ` ) of 0.5 (p. 8). When AI makes some instances cheap, the instances that people still perform become the bottleneck. The paper calls them "the weak link, so their expenditure share rises" (p. 13). In plain words, the economy cannot use the extra AI output without more of the human work around it. "At` σ` = 0.5, half of every gain is spent on more of the same task" (p. 15).


**What the extreme numbers mean.** In the extreme scenario, the cognitive wage is 11.5% below the no-AI path. Because wages grow about 2% a year without AI, "cognitive wages are slightly lower in 2030 than in mid-2026" in absolute terms (p. 35). Wages in all other occupations, "where labor is now comparatively scarce, are 33.6 percent higher" (p. 35).


The model leaves out robotics: it considers "only the effects of AI on cognitive tasks" and does not allow "rapid advances in robotics and their effects on physical tasks" (p. 5). So the all-other group is untouched by AI by assumption. In our reading, that assumption is a large part of why the all-other wage can rise 33.6%: no machine competes for that work in the model, while the economy around it grows by a third. ## 📉 What Is the Labor Share, and Why Does It Fall?


**The labor share is the part of national income that goes to workers as pay. The capital share is the rest, paid to the owners of machines, buildings, software and compute. In the paper, the US labor share starts at 60% and falls to 59.4%, 56.1% or 45.2% by 2030, because automated tasks move their wage bill to capital (Table 3, p. 31).**


### The 60% is a model setting, not a measurement


The starting value is a choice of the authors. Table 1 lists the "base-period labor share" as 0.60, and its stated basis is "conventional value for the U.S." (p. 23). The text repeats it: "labor earns 60 percent of income before AI" (p. 25). The base period of the model is 2024, and its paths are anchored in mid-2026 (Table 1, p. 23).

The chart, "Labor and capital share of income in 2030" (Table 3, p. 31), shows the same two shares as bars, on an axis that starts at 0.


**Three forces move the share.** The paper writes that "The labor share responds through three channels" (p. 13). Two push it down and one pushes it back up:


1. **Automation.** "The entire wage bill of an automated instance moves to capital, however small the cost saving that motivated the switch" (p. 13). New tasks for people (reinstatement) offset part of that fall.
2. **The weak link.** The tasks that people keep become dearer relative to the automated ones. Tasks are complements, so spending does not move away from them in full: "They are the weak link, so their expenditure share rises" (p. 13). This force adds back to the labor share.
3. **Dearer capital.** When the return to capital rises, "capital's instances become dearer relative to labor's and expenditure follows them, which lowers the labor share" (p. 13).


In our reading, the first force explains why the share can fall fast. A firm that moves a task to AI to save a cent still moves the whole pay for that task to the capital column.


**Four points in four years.** In the substantial scenario the labor share falls from 60% to 56% and the capital share rises from 40% to 44%. The authors call it "a shift of four points in four years, only slightly less than the entire decline in the U.S. labor share over the four decades after 1980" (p. 33). For that four-decade decline, the paper cites Karabarbounis and Neiman (2014) (p. 33).


The extreme scenario goes further: "A full 15 percent of GDP moves from being paid to labor to being captured as a return on investment" (p. 35).


**A falling share does not mean falling pay.** A share is a ratio. Pay is a level. In the extreme scenario, labor income in 2030 is 0.5% above the no-AI path (Table 3, p. 31). The paper shows why: "the labor share falls by a quarter while GDP rises by a third, and 0.45 × 1.32 ≈ 0.60" (p. 35). Total labor income is "almost exactly what it would have been without AI" (p. 35).


Labor income is also above the no-AI path in the modest (+0.6%) and substantial (+1.4%) scenarios, while the share falls in both (Table 3, p. 31).

## 🧭 How Will We Know Which Scenario We Are In?


**The paper's test is to measure four inputs: the affected mass, the diffusion share, the productivity gain per task, and how long a displaced worker takes to find a new job (p. 39). The scenarios start from the same mid-2026 readings of reach and use (p. 27), so the data that separate them arrive mostly after 2027 (pp. 4 and 38).**


**Why the data cannot tell yet.** The authors write that "the scenarios therefore make statements about data we will observe over the coming years, and those data will tell us which scenario we are in" (p. 39). Two facts explain the wait:


- **The scenarios share a start.** Each path of the affected mass and the diffusion share runs through the same mid-2026 reading, so "the scenarios coincide at mid-2026" (p. 27).
- **They separate late.** "Almost all of the divergence comes after 2027, a year and a half from the mid-2026 anchor" (p. 38). The introduction says the same (p. 4).


Up to the paper's date, September 2026, the labor market effects of AI in the macroeconomic data "have been relatively muted even as measured AI usage has grown rapidly" (p. 4). The paper reads that fact two ways: the economy is in a modest scenario, or it is "only at the very beginning of a more extreme scenario" (p. 4).

## 📚 How Does This Paper Compare With Other AI Jobs Estimates?


**Published AI jobs estimates measure different quantities, so they cannot be ranked against each other.** Some count jobs exposed to AI, some count jobs at risk, some estimate extra productivity growth or a GDP level, some measure what has happened in the data, and the Anthropic Institute paper gives conditional scenario outcomes. A 47% and a 6% answer different questions.


### Why the numbers do not line up


Take three figures. Frey and Osborne found that "about 47 per cent of total US employment is at risk" ([Oxford Martin School](https://www.oxfordmartin.ox.ac.uk/publications/the-future-of-employment) , 2013). The IMF found that "Almost 40 percent of global employment is exposed to AI" ([IMF SDN/2024/001](https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/sdn/2024/english/sdnea2024001.pdf) , January 2024). Forrester forecast that 6.1% of US jobs will be lost to AI and automation by 2030 ([Forrester](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/ai-and-automation-will-take-6-of-us-jobs-by-2030/) , January 13, 2026).


Those three numbers do not contradict each other, because each one counts a different thing:


- **Exposed** means AI touches the tasks of a job. The IMF note itself says that of the exposed jobs in advanced economies, "about half may be negatively affected by AI", while the rest could gain productivity.
- **At risk** means a job has a high estimated probability of computerisation. The Oxford page gives no date by which the risk is realized.
- **Lost** means a job that no longer exists. Forrester counts 10.4 million jobs, and it also writes: "We see AI strongly influencing jobs (20%) more commonly than replacing them (6.1%)".


The Anthropic Institute paper adds a fourth kind of number: a model output at chosen inputs. Its authors write that published estimates of productivity effects "span orders of magnitude", and that forecasts of employment effects "range from negligible to catastrophic" (p. 3). Their stated aim is to put all of these views into one framework, so that each becomes a set of inputs.

This part is our reading. The paper does not discuss tellers, spreadsheets or operators. It does set three inputs that these cases illustrate (Table 1, pp. 23 and 24, and pp. 27 and 28):

Table 1 calls these values "scenario assumptions" and notes that Acemoglu and Restrepo (2019) estimated 0.5 (p. 24). Only the modest value rests on that estimate: in their work "new tasks roughly kept pace with automated ones" from 1947 to 1987 and "ran at about half of them" from 1987 to 2017 (p. 28). The paper defines the input "in the spirit of" Acemoglu and Restrepo (2019) and Autor et al. (2024) (p. 11). The 60% of 2018 jobs in new titles and the 600,000 new accountant jobs are examples of reinstatement. In the model, "The new tasks belong to the cognitive occupations, whose tasks were automated" (p. 11), as the accountant jobs did.
- **Search discount (` μ` ).** How hard it is for a displaced worker to find a job in the other group of occupations: 0.17 in the modest scenario, 0.08 in the substantial and 0.04 in the extreme (p. 28). The operator case shows the cost that this input cannot fully hold. The paper says so: a worker who moves to the other group "earns that group's wage at once, with no discount for lost tenure or occupation-specific skills" (p. 5). Incumbent operators did take such a discount.
- **Automation share (` ψ` ).** The share of AI use that does a task outright, not with a person: 0.50, 0.75 or 0.90. The paper anchors it on the Anthropic Economic Index, where about half of use on Claude.ai and about three quarters on the API looks like automation (pp. 27 and 28). The ATM did part of the teller's job, as an assistant does part of a task. Mobile banking removed the visit, closer to full automation.

### The Yale Budget Lab: the job mix is changing, but not because of AI


The Yale Budget Lab measures how fast the mix of occupations changes after a new technology, with November 2022 as the baseline for AI and January 1984 and January 1996 for computers and the internet. Its January 28, 2026 update found that "While the occupational mix is changing more quickly than it has in the past, it is not a large difference and predates the widespread introduction of AI in the workforce" ([Yale Budget Lab](https://budgetlab.yale.edu/sites/default/files/page_to_pdf/1334/publication_1334.pdf) ). The government shutdown meant that BLS did not collect CPS data for October 2025, so the lab omits that month.


The tracker is a live page. Its version updated on September 15, 2026, with August 2026 CPS microdata, reached the same result: "Churn across occupations, AI exposure among the unemployed, and usage data all remain flat, lie within historical ranges, or continue along pre-AI trends" ([Yale Budget Lab tracker](https://budgetlab.yale.edu/sites/default/files/page_to_pdf/1419/publication_1419.pdf) ). The note also shows how far use lags capability. In Computer and Math jobs, "Claude currently covers just 33% of all tasks", against a theoretical scope for language models of 94%, which the note takes from the task ratings of Eloundou and coauthors.

## 📜 What Did "Machines of Loving Grace" Say About AI and Work?


**"Machines of Loving Grace" is an essay by Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, published in October 2024. The essay sketches "what a world with powerful AI might look like if everything goes right". It is a conditional prediction, true only "if everything goes right", and its clock starts when powerful AI arrives, not on the day the essay appeared.**


The essay covers five areas: biology and physical health, neuroscience and mental health, economic development and poverty, peace and governance, and work and meaning (introduction). Work gets a short section. The author writes that "the brevity of this section is not at all to be taken as a sign that I don't take these issues seriously" (section 5, "Work and meaning").


Four framing facts keep the essay in its place:


- **It is a best case.** The essay says its content is "unavoidably going to consist of guesses", and adds: "Everything I'm saying could very easily be wrong" (introduction).
- **Its clock starts later.** Powerful AI "could come as early as 2026, though there are also ways it could take much longer". The essay's 5 to 10 years are counted from powerful AI, which it calls "the threshold at which the 5-10 year clock starts counting" ("Basic assumptions and framework").
- **It is one person's view.** The paper discussed above is by five economists, and its title page says the views are the authors' and "do not necessarily represent the views of Anthropic" (p. 1).
- **The two texts do not cite each other.** The paper never names the essay. It uses the phrase "powerful AI" once, in its last sentence, where the authors say they built the framework "to inform the debate over how society can best manage the transition to powerful AI" (p. 39).


The diagram shows two separate clocks. The essay's window opens only when powerful AI exists, which the essay says could come as early as 2026 or much later ("Basic assumptions and framework"). The paper's clock carries its three scenarios. The paper's window runs from mid-2026 to the start of 2030 (pp. 3 and 5). Nothing in either text joins the two clocks. The last box of the essay clock holds only "if everything goes right".


### What is powerful AI?


**Powerful AI is the essay's name for the system that starts its clock. Amodei writes "I dislike the term AGI", and a footnote explains that he finds AGI "an imprecise term that has gathered a lot of sci-fi baggage and hype"** ("Basic assumptions and framework", footnote 3). The essay defines powerful AI by six properties instead of by a test score.

2 Works through every remote interface "all the 'interfaces' available to a human working virtually"


3 Does long tasks on its own "tasks that take hours, days, or weeks to complete"


4 Controls tools, but has no body "does not have a physical embodiment"


5 Runs many fast copies "run millions of instances of it", at "roughly 10x-100x human speed"


6 Copies work alone or as a team "Each of these million copies can act independently on unrelated tasks"


*The six properties of powerful AI, in the essay's order. Source: "Machines of Loving Grace", section "Basic assumptions and framework".*


Property 5 carries its own limit. The essay adds that the model "may however be limited by the response time of the physical world or of software it interacts with". That sentence points ahead to the limiting factors below. **"A country of geniuses in a datacenter" is the essay's one-line summary of powerful AI: millions of copies of a model that is smarter than top experts, each able to work alone or with the others.** Right after the six properties, the essay writes: "We could summarize this as a 'country of geniuses in a datacenter'" ("Basic assumptions and framework").


The phrase describes a capability, not a date. The essay also rejects the idea that such a system changes the world in days: "Even a new country of geniuses would hit up against these limits", and "Intelligence may be very powerful, but it isn't magic fairy dust" (same section). **The "compressed 21st century" is the essay's name for its main claim about science. In the essay's words: "my basic prediction is that AI-enabled biology and medicine will allow us to compress the progress that human biologists would have achieved over the next 50-100 years into 5-10 years"** (section 1, "Biology and health").

### What are the marginal returns to intelligence?


**The marginal returns to intelligence are the essay's way to ask how much a smarter mind helps a given task. The essay says "we should be talking about the marginal returns to intelligence" and frames the question as "how much does being smarter help with this task, and on what timescale?"** ("Basic assumptions and framework").


The answer has two halves, and both matter. Intelligence is "initially heavily bottlenecked by the other factors of production, but over time intelligence itself increasingly routes around the other factors, even if they never fully dissolve" (same section). The first half is a short-run brake. The second half is a long-run release. The essay names five factors that do the braking.

A footnote applies the same idea to AI research itself. AI that builds better AI "might (in fact, probably will) occur", but its effect "will be smaller than you might imagine, precisely because of the 'decreasing marginal returns to intelligence'" (footnote 10). The essay also credits the scaling hypothesis and the bitter lesson for its view of how intelligence works (section 2). ### The 90% paragraph, and the long run


**On work, the essay gives a short-run case and a different long-run case.** The short-run case: "As long as AI is only better at 90% of a given job, the other 10% will cause humans to become highly leveraged" (section 5). The essay adds that new human jobs can grow until the "10%" "expands to continue to employ almost everyone".


The short-run case rests on comparative advantage. The essay writes that "even if AI can do 100% of things better than humans, but it remains inefficient or expensive at some tasks", the "logic of comparative advantage continues to apply". It names one area where people keep an edge: "One area humans are likely to maintain a relative (or even absolute) advantage for a significant time is the physical world." Its conclusion: "the human economy may continue to make sense even a little past the point where we reach 'a country of geniuses in a datacenter'" (all section 5).


The long-run case reverses the short-run one. Amodei writes that in the long run AI will "become so broadly effective and so cheap that this will no longer apply". He continues: at that point "our current economic setup will no longer make sense", and society will need "a broader societal conversation about how the economy should be organized" (section 5).


The essay names possible answers and commits to none:


Option in the essay The essay's words (section 5)


A large universal basic income "although I suspect that will only be a small part of a solution"


An economy run by AI systems "a capitalist economy of AI systems, which then give out resources" to humans


Reputation as currency "Perhaps the economy runs on Whuffie points."


People stay valuable after all "in some way not anticipated by the usual economic models"


*The options for a post-work economy that the essay lists. Source: "Machines of Loving Grace", section 5, "Work and meaning".*


The essay is careful about all four. It writes that "All of these solutions have tons of possible problems" and that "exploitative or dystopian directions are clearly also possible and have to be prevented". It ends the section with "Much more could be written about these questions" (section 5). On meaning, as apart from income, its view is plain: "I think meaning comes mostly from human relationships and connection, not from economic labor" (section 5).


### The 20% "dream scenario" for the developing world


**The essay's 20% growth number is a goal for poor countries, not a number for rich ones.** The text says a dream scenario "would be 20% annual GDP growth rate in the developing world", "with 10% each coming from AI-enabled economic decisions and the natural spread of AI-accelerated technologies" (section 3, "Economic development and poverty").


The essay grounds the number in history and then hedges it:


- **The precedent.** Several East Asian economies "achieved sustained ~10% annual real GDP growth rates" in the late 20th century (section 3).
- **The target.** If achieved, the 20% rate "would bring sub-Saharan Africa to the current per-capita GDP of China in 5-10 years" (section 3).
- **The hedge.** "Again, this is a dream scenario, not what happens by default" (section 3).
- **The risk.** AI and automation "also pose challenges for economic development, particularly for countries that haven't yet industrialized" (section 3).


On inequality inside rich countries, the essay asks for effort, not trust: "here is another place where we collectively have to do all we can to ensure a fair society" (section 3).

### Growth: two numbers that measure different things


**The essay's 20% and the paper's 15.4% look close, but they are different objects.** The 20% is a goal for the developing world, in a window that opens only after powerful AI exists (section 3). The 15.4% is the GDP growth rate of the United States over the twelve months to 2030 in the paper's extreme scenario, which the authors describe as "unprecedented" (p. 34).


Three differences keep the two apart:


Difference Essay (20%) Paper (15.4%)


Place Poor countries The United States


Status A "dream scenario" One model output at chosen inputs, no probability (p. 3)


Source of growth AI-guided policy and the spread of new technology, 10 points each (section 3) Mostly cheaper cognitive tasks, with a small ideas channel (p. 4)


For scale, the paper notes that a sustained 15.4% rate would double income per person every five years, against every 35 years in the US over the past century (p. 34).


### The engine: discovery against automation


**In our reading, the sharpest contrast is the engine of growth.** In our reading, much of the essay's upside rests on discovery: more and faster breakthroughs in biology and medicine. In the paper, AI raises output mostly by doing a share of cognitive task instances more cheaply. Research is a second channel, and by 2030 it is small.


The paper's numbers on that second channel:


- The authors call the size of the innovation channel "One surprising finding": the growth speedup "is relatively minor, even in the extreme change scenario" (p. 4).
- The reason: automating research raises research input, "but research remains bottlenecked by physical tasks" (p. 4).
- By the start of 2030, the stock of ideas is 0.07%, 0.20% or 0.61% above the no-AI path in the three scenarios (Table 3, p. 31).
- The authors add that the model leaves out some feedback between research and automation, "so the innovation effects here are likely a lower bound" (p. 4).


In our reading, the two texts agree on the cause. The essay says intelligence is "initially heavily bottlenecked by the other factors of production", and the first factor it lists is the speed of the outside world. The paper's ideas channel is small for a similar reason, and only over a four-year window. Neither text says the bottleneck is permanent: the essay expects intelligence to route around it over time, and the paper calls its own estimate a lower bound.


### Where the essay and the model point the same way


The side-by-side table above pairs lines of the essay with inputs or outputs of the model. The pairing is our reading.


The pairs show agreement in direction, not a test. The paper does not test the essay, and it could not: the paper stops at 2030, and by the essay's own definition its clock has not started until powerful AI exists. In our reading, one pair also shows a gap. The essay's 10% keeps "almost everyone" employed through new jobs. The paper's extreme scenario sets new human tasks per automated task to 0 (Table 1, p. 24), so in that column the 10% has no room to grow.


### The essay's five limits, mapped to the model (our reading)


The essay's five limiting factors and the paper's parameters were written for different purposes. The mapping below is our reading, not a claim by either author.


Read the diagram in three groups. First, the speed of the outside world sits closest to two paper inputs: how fast AI spreads across task instances (p. 10) and the physical bottleneck on research (p. 4). Second, constraints from humans sit closest to the labor market frictions: how hard it is to switch occupations, and how slowly the cognitive wage adjusts (p. 28). Third, the need for data, intrinsic complexity and physical laws have no parameter in the model. The paper's horizon is short, and it leaves out robotics and physical tasks (p. 5).


The paper also has a limit that the essay does not list: capital. The paper sets the elasticity of capital supply at 3 (p. 26). Over a few years, the economy cannot add capital at once, so part of the gain goes to the owners of capital (p. 6). When capital is scarce, the average wage can even fall below the no-AI path (p. 37). The section on capital and wage rigidity gives those numbers.

## 🧬 What a Worker, a Founder and a Small Team Can Do


**In the paper's own terms, the cost of AI to cognitive workers shows up as a lower relative wage, higher unemployment, or a mix: "The cost to cognitive workers is a combination of a lower relative wage and higher unemployment" (p. 38). Augmented use keeps a task with the worker (p. 11).** Those two facts frame every step below.


The paper gives four facts that matter for a plan:


- **Wages or jobs.** In the extreme scenario, cognitive unemployment runs from 2.6% with flexible wages to 24.0% with rigid wages (Table 6, p. 38). The cost moves between pay and jobs. It does not disappear.
- **Augmentation keeps the work.** "The gain on an augmented instance is available only if a worker performs it" (p. 11).
- **Some workers cross more easily.** Unemployed sales and office workers take a job outside the cognitive occupations 28% of the time, managers and professionals only 10% of the time (p. 28).
- **People disagree on what AI can build.** Only 24% of US adults say AI can already build a working software product as well as a skilled professional, and 27% say it never will (Figure 1, p. 29).

### For a worker


**For a worker, our reading of the paper is simple: stay on the augmented side of the task, and know your own numbers.** The paper measures AI by the share of tasks it affects and the share of instances where it is used (p. 10). A worker can track the same two numbers for one job.


### For a founder


**For a founder, our reading is that the paper's distribution numbers are a reason to own the system, not only to rent out hours.** In the extreme scenario, capital income is 81.4% above the no-AI path while labor income is 0.5% above it (Table 3, p. 31). In the paper, capital means machines and compute, with no split between them (pp. 5 and 26), and the paper gives no advice to founders. In our reading, a small company that builds its own tools and automations holds a piece of the side that grows.

**For a small team, our reading is that people keep the decisions and the approvals, and agents take the routine steps.** The paper's scenarios differ in how many new human tasks appear per automated task: 0.5, 0.25 or 0 (Table 1, p. 24). ## 💬 Frequently Asked Questions About AI and Jobs in 2030


Will AI cause mass unemployment by 2030?


Nobody knows, and a September 2026 economic model does not claim to. In an Anthropic Institute paper, US unemployment at the start of 2030 is 3.9%, 4.6% or 11.9% for all workers in three scenarios, against 3.8% with no AI. The authors attach no probability to any scenario, and labor studies with data through August 2026 show no clear AI effect.


Did Anthropic forecast unemployment from AI?


No. The paper "Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI" says "The scenarios are not predictions, and we attach no probabilities to them". Its title page says that the views are those of the five authors and do not necessarily represent the views of Anthropic or The Anthropic Institute. Each number is a model output at chosen inputs.


What are the three AI scenarios for 2030?


Modest, substantial and extreme change. At the start of 2030, GDP is 1.6%, 8.3% or 32.4% above an economy with no AI. Cognitive employment is 0.5%, 3.9% or 21.5% below its mid-2026 level, and the unemployment rate of workers who began in cognitive occupations is 2.9%, 4.5% or 17.9%. The two rows have different bases.


Will AI lower the labor share of income?


In the paper's scenarios, yes. The labor share falls from 60% to 59.4%, 56.1% or 45.2% by 2030, because an automated task moves its whole wage bill to capital. A falling share is not falling pay: in the extreme case, total labor income still ends 0.5% above the no-AI path, while capital income is 81.4% above it.


Will AI raise or cut wages?


Both, for different groups. In the extreme scenario, wages in cognitive occupations (management, professional, sales and office jobs) are 11.5% below the no-AI path at the start of 2030, and wages in all other occupations are 33.6% above it. The model leaves out robotics, so AI does not compete with the second group.


How big would a transfer to displaced workers need to be?


In the extreme scenario, the paper sizes it at about 9% of GDP, roughly the size of Social Security and Medicare combined. That transfer keeps cognitive workers' income at its no-AI level and leaves the rest of the economy more than 20% ahead. The authors add that transfers of that scale in response to technological change have no precedent.


What do Americans expect AI to do to jobs by 2030?


The authors surveyed 10,980 US adults from August 11 to 23, 2026. For the 3,259 who answered all five questions, they ran the model on each person's answers. The median outcome is close to the substantial scenario: GDP 8.6% above the no-AI path and cognitive employment 4.2% lower than in mid-2026.


How does this paper compare with other AI job estimates?


The estimates measure different things, so they do not rank. Frey and Osborne put 47% of US jobs at risk of computerisation in 2013. The IMF found almost 40% of global jobs exposed to AI in 2024. Forrester forecast 6.1% of US jobs lost by 2030. The Anthropic Institute paper gives scenario outcomes at chosen inputs.


How will we know which AI scenario we are in?


The paper names inputs that people can measure: the share of tasks AI can do, how widely it is used, the productivity gain per task, and how long a displaced worker takes to find a new job. The scenarios separate mostly after 2027, and in September 2026 the authors wrote that the answer may become clearer within a year or two.


What is powerful AI in Machines of Loving Grace?


Powerful AI is the term that Dario Amodei used in his October 2024 essay instead of AGI. It means a model that is smarter than a Nobel Prize winner across most fields, works through every interface of a remote worker, does tasks of hours to weeks on its own, and runs as millions of fast copies.


What does a country of geniuses in a datacenter mean?


It is the summary phrase for powerful AI in the essay Machines of Loving Grace. It pictures millions of copies of a model that is smarter than top experts, each able to work alone or with the others, all running in a datacenter. The essay uses it as a definition of a capability, not as a date.


What is the compressed 21st century?


It is the idea, from Machines of Loving Grace, that after powerful AI arrives, biology and medicine could make the progress of 50 to 100 years in 5 to 10 years. The essay calls it a prediction inside a vision of what happens if everything goes right. The clock starts when powerful AI exists, not in 2024.
